posts.caption:
Marathon mileage for runners: what the research actually says.

119,452 Strava runners. Faster marathoners did more of the ‘slow’ work.

Review your last four weeks: total distance, easy volume and recovery. Build from your own tolerated workload, rather than jumping to a faster group’s average.

Source: Muniz-Pumares et al. · Sports Medicine · 2025. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39616560/

Download PR Pacer at prpacer.com.

#PRPacer #MarathonTraining #RunningResearch #EasyMiles #RunnerTok
altText: 119,452 Strava runners. Faster marathoners did more of the ‘slow’ work.
151,813 marathons. Sixteen weeks of training. The fastest group, finishing in 2:00–2:30, averaged about 107 km/week. The 4:30–5:00 group averaged about 35 km/week.

Most of the extra volume was low intensity. Faster groups accumulated more low-intensity running. The study used three zones, not your watch’s five-zone labels. Absolute time in harder zones was comparatively similar.
Those are groups, not a prescription. The study used 30-minute finish-time groups, not exact sub-2:45 versus sub-4 cohorts. Association cannot prove that copying the mileage causes the same result.
Audit what you can repeat. Review your last four weeks: total distance, easy volume and recovery. Build from your own tolerated workload, rather than jumping to a faster group’s average.

#PRPacer #RunningInjury #LongRun #TrainingLoad #RunnerTok
altText: Your weekly mileage can look sensible. One run can still be a spike.
5,205 runners. 588,071 sessions. Overuse injury rates were higher when one run exceeded the runner’s longest run in the previous 30 days by more than 10%.
A weekly total can hide one big leap. Compare a proposed long run with your recent longest run, not only with your weekly mileage. This is a different question from the familiar weekly ‘10% rule’.
10% is not an injury force field. This observational result does not prove a safe threshold for everyone. A smaller increase can still be too much, especially when intensity or recovery also changes.
Check the biggest session first. Before extending the long run, write down your longest completed run in the past month. Consider the distance jump, recent consistency and how you recovered.

altText: Running beside someone felt easier. The clock didn’t agree.

Feeling better is not the same as running faster. Nine of eleven male runners said a 5K felt easier with another runner. Yet the study found no significant difference in finish time, pacing or measured perceived exertion.
A running buddy can still make the day better. Enjoyment and company are worthwhile. A stronger performance claim requires a stronger result than ‘it felt easier afterward’.
A small study does not settle every group run. The protocol used eleven men and specific positions for a second runner. It cannot rule out benefits in other settings or populations.
Choose the purpose of the group run. Run together for company or a shared session plan. If testing a performance claim, compare actual comparable results rather than only the memory of effort.

altText: Four million race records. The wall still isn’t a diagnosis.
The dataset measured sustained late-race slowing. Researchers used more than four million marathon records to define and examine a pacing-based version of ‘hitting the wall’.
A split chart shows what happened, not every cause. Fueling, early effort, conditions and preparation are worth reviewing. A late slowdown by itself cannot tell you which factor dominated.
Race records are not glycogen measurements. The analysis cannot diagnose the biology behind each runner’s slowdown. ‘The wall’ is a useful performance description, not a complete explanation.

Reading research for runners: what the research actually says.

A huge study still can’t prove your training plan works.

Who was studied? What was actually measured? Was it an observation or an experiment? Save those questions for the next ‘science proves’ running post.

Source: Muniz-Pumares et al. · Sports Medicine · 2025. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39616560/

Download PR Pacer at prpacer.com.

#PRPacer #SportsScience #EvidenceBasedRunning #RunningResearch #RunnerTok
altText: A huge study still can’t prove your training plan works.

Big data improves description, not automatic causation. The Strava analysis compared existing training and marathon outcomes. Runners were not randomly assigned to copy another performance group’s mileage.
Ask what changed and who chose it. A correlation can reflect experience, available training time, fitness and other differences. More data does not make those explanations disappear.
This is not a reason to ignore useful evidence. Observational studies can reveal patterns worth testing. Their limits should shape the claim, not be hidden behind the sample size.
